Abia.ete: Borrowed from Latin Abīa, from Ancient Greek Ἀβῑᾱ́ (Abīā́), from Hebrew אֲבִיָה (ʾĂḇiyyā́, “worshipper of Jah”)

Abraham.ete: Learned borrowing from Late Latin Ābraham, from Ancient Greek Ἀβραάμ (Abraám), from Hebrew אַבְרָהָם (aḇrāˈhām, “Abraham”).

Adalar.ete: From Old High German Adalheri, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalaheri, from *aþal (“noble”) + *hari (“army”). Equivalent to Adel + Heer.

Adalbert.ete: From Middle High German Adalbërt, from Old High German Adalbërht, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalaberht.

Adalger.ete: From Old High German Adalgēr, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalagaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *Aþalagaizaz. Equivalent to Adel (“nobility”) + Ger (“throwing spear”). Cognate with English Alger, Elgar.

q: „Aus einer urkundlich nicht benannten Gemahlin hatte erwähnter Adalper Niger II., wie es scheint, nur einen einzigen Sohn, Niger II., welcher, als der jüngere, häufig Negerle benannt wurde, erzeugt, der aber im blühendsten Mannesalter, noch vor dem Vater Adalper schon um’s Jahr 1370 dem Tode als Beute fiel, aus einer ungenannten Gemahlin einen urkundlich nachweisbaren Sohn, Leonard, hinterlassend; …“

P. Justinian Ladurner: Die Familie der Edlen von Negri di S. Pietro. Genealogische Nachrichten ueber die Edlen von Negri di S. Pietro. Druck der Wagner’schen Universitäts-Buchdruckerei, Innsbruck 1874. Seite 15

Adalwin.ete: From Old High German Adalwin, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalawini, equivalent to Old High German adal (“noble”) + Old High German wini (“friend”), cognate with English Alwin and Dutch Adelwijn.

Adam.ete: Borrowed from Latin Adam, from Ancient Greek Ἀδάμ (Adám), from Hebrew אָדָם (ʾāḏām, “man, soil, light brown”).

Adele.ete: Borrowed from French Adèle, from a Germanic root meaning “noble”. Compare edel and Adel.

Adeler.ete: From Old High German adal (“noble”) + heri (“army”).

Adelgunde.ete: From Old High German adal (“noble”) + gunt.

Adelheid.ete: From Old High German Adalheid, popularized by Adelaide of Italy, a 10th-century Frankish saint and wife of Otto the Great. Cognate to English Adelaide and Alice. Doublet of Alice.
Adelheid.et: Dérivé de Adel, avec le suffixe -heit.

Adelmar.ete: From Old High German *Adalmār, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalamār.

Adolf.ete: From Old High German adal (“noble”) + wolf (“wolf”).
Adolf.et: Du vieux haut allemand Adalwolf, de adal (« noble ») et wolf (« loup »).

Adrian.ete: From Latin Hadriānus, ultimately from Etruscan 𐌇𐌀𐌕𐌓𐌉𐌀 (hatria).

Adulf.ete: From Old High German adal (“noble”) + wolf (“wolf”).

Agatha.ete: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Ἀγαθή (Agathḗ), from Ancient Greek ἀγαθός (agathós, “good”).

q: „Der wilde voreilige Friedrich Mannsfeld murmelte Bestätigung dessen, was Gebhard in seinen Augen zu lesen glaubte, der alte General nannte den Namen Carl Truchseß, mit zur Erde gesenktem Blick, und Agnesens Vater, der all diese Zeit über geschwiegen hatte, fragte mit einem tiefen Seufzer, ob dies die Zeit sey, auf Heyrathswerbungen zu denken?“
Benedikte Naubert: Gebhard Truchses von Waldburg, Churfürst von Cöln, oder die astrologischen Fürsten, Erster Theil, 1792, S. 251 f.
Agnes.ete: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἁγνή (Hagnḗ), coming from Ancient Greek ἁγνός (hagnós, “pure, chaste”)

Aische.ete: Borrowed from Turkish Ayşe, from Arabic عَائِشَة (ʕāʔiša). The use as a common noun is due to the name's commonness among Turkish immigrants, possibly reinforced by the unrelated noun Ische (“gal, chick”).

Albert.ete: From Middle High German Adalbërt, from Old High German Adalbërht, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalaberht.

Albin.ete: Borrowed from Latin Albīnus, partly merged with Germanic Albwin, the German equivalent of English Alvin.

Albrecht.ete: From Middle High German Adalbërt, from Old High German Adalbërht, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalaberht.

Albuin.ete: From Old High German alb (“elf”) + wini (“friend”), cognate to English Alvin.

q: „Vor fünf Jahren war's. Als Graf Alexander Murány Hochzeit hielt.“
Emil Marriot: Anständige Frauen. Ullstein, Berlin/Wien 1913, Seite 10.
Alexander.et: Du latin Alexander, emprunté au grec ancien Ἀλέξανδρος, Aléxandros.

Alexandra.ete: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Ἀλεξάνδρα (Alexándra), from ἀλέξω (aléxō, “to defend”) + ἀνδρ- (andr-), the stem of ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”). Feminine form of Alexander.

Alfred.ete: Borrowed from English Alfred, from Old English Ælfræd.

Algerd.ete: From Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌷𐍃 (alhs, “holy temple”) + 𐌲𐌰𐍂𐌳𐍃 (gards, “protector”) or Old High German alah + garda, and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *alhs and *gardaz; cognate to Lithuanian Algerdas, Algė, and German Algimund.

Algimund.ete: From Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌷𐍃 (alhs, “holy temple”) + 𐌼𐌿𐌽𐌳𐍃 (munds, “power of mind, aspiration”) or Old High German alah (“holy temple”) + munt (“protector”), and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *alhs (“temple; sanctuary”) and *mundō (“protection, security”).

Alice.ete: Borrowed from English Alice. Doublet of Adelheid.

Altman.et: Composé de alt et de Mann, littéralement « vieil homme » ; comparer avec Seneca en latin.

Alwin.ete: From Old High German Adalwin, from Proto-West Germanic *Aþalawini, equivalent to Old High German adal (“noble”) + Old High German wini (“friend”), cognate with English Alwin, English Alvin, and Dutch Adelwijn.

Amelia.ete: Latinization of names derived from Proto-Germanic *amalą (“vigor, bravery”). For the first element, compare *ammōną (“to bother, irritate”).

Amelie.ete: Derived from Proto-Germanic compound names beginning with the element *amal (“vigor”).

q: „›Wir sind allein,‹ sagte Amrei während des Tanzes und gleich darauf spürte sie den heißen Athem des Tänzers, der ihr erwiederte: ›O wären wir allein, allein auf der Welt!…‹“
Berthold Auerbach: Barfüßele. Fünfzehnter unveränderter Abdruck. Verlag der J. G. Cotta’schen Buchhandlung, Stuttgart 1873. Seite 134

Anatol.ete: Borrowed from Latin Anatolius, from Ancient Greek ἀνατολή (anatolḗ, “sunrise”).

Andreas.et: Du latin Andreas, dérivé du grec ancien Ἀνδρέας.

q: „Kritikus[:] Und Du bist einer von den Liebes-Engeln (er will Angela küssen, und bekömmt eine Ohrfeige.)“
Joseph Freiherr von Eichendorff: Krieg den Philistern. Dramatisches Mährchen in fünf Abentheuern. Bei Ferdinand Dümmler, Berlin 1824. Seite 164

Ännchen.ete: From Middle High German Ennechin. By surface analysis, Anne + -chen.

q: „Noch vor einem Weilchen dort in dem Zimmer waren wir allein, das Annerl mit mir. Und ich habe sie geküßt, geküßt – habe – ich – sie auf ihren Mund, ihre Ohren, ihre Schultern. Mein Gott und Herr!“
Franz Kafka: Beschreibung eines Kampfes. Prag zwischen 1904 und 1910 (ältere Rechtschreibung) .

Annina.ete: Borrowed from Italian Annina, made known in Germany by 19th and 20th century opera characters.

Ansbald.ete: From Old High German ans (“god, deity”) + bald (“bold”).

Anselm.ete: From Old High German ans (“god”) + Old High German helm (“helmet”).

q: „Da warf ich denn die Feder hin und eilte ins Bett, um wenigstens von dem glücklichen Anselmus und der holden Serpentina zu träumen.“
„Der goldne Topf“, von E.T.A. Hoffmann, 1814
„Hier nun trat Ansfried öffentlich auf und hielt eine Untersuchung über das Abendmahl.“
„Berengarius Turonensis: oder eine Sammlung ihn betreffender Briefe“, von Hans Friedrich Georg Julius Sudendorf, F. und A. Perthes, 1850
Ansfried.ete: From Old High German ans (“god, deity”) + fridu (“peace”).

Ansgar.ete: From Old High German ans (“god”) + Old High German gēr (“spear”). Cognate with Faroese and Icelandic Ásgeir, Swedish and Danish Asger, Norwegian Nynorsk Åsgeir, and English Oscar.

Answald.ete: From Old High German Answalt, from Proto-Germanic *Ansuwaldaz. Cognate with Faroese and Icelandic Ásvaldur, Norwegian Åsvald, English Oswald, Italian Ansaldo, and Italian, Spanish, and Portuguese Osvaldo.

Anton.ete: Borrowed from Latin Antōnius. Cognate to English Anthony.

Antonin.ete: Borrowed from Latin Antōnīnus, in many cases via Czech Antonín.

q: „Ariowist gefiel sich in ihren fruchtbaren Fluren, und zog immer mehrere Landsleute an sich.“
„Deutsches Land und Deutsches Volk, Band 2, Teil 1“, von Johann Christoph Friedrich Guts Muths, J. A. Jacobi, Streudelschen, 1820

Armin.ete: Borrowed from Latin Arminius (“name of a Cherusci chieftain”), possibly from Proto-Germanic *ermunaz.

Arnd.ete: Contraction of Arnold, Arnwald. Compare Middle Dutch Aernt.

Arnold.ete: From Old High German arn (“eagle”, cf. Aar), + Old High German waltan (“ruler”, cf. walten).
Arnold.et: Du haut-germanique arn « l’aigle », et waldan « gouverner ».

Arnulf.ete: From Old High German *Arnwolf, from Proto-Germanic *Arôwulfaz, equivalent to Old High German arn (“eagle”) + wulf (“wolf”).

Arthur.ete: Borrowed from English in the 18th century.

Ashelm.ete: From Old High German ans (“god”) + Old High German helm (“helmet”).

Aster.ete: Borrowed from Latin astēr (“star”). Doublet of Star and Stern.

Astrid.ete: Borrowed from modern Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian, Danish) Astrid.

Atze.ete: Attested since the end of the 18th century and originally probably from the Netherlands. While most likely a diminutive, it is unknown which given name Atze has developed out of; it likely emerged in different dialects independently. Candidates include Andreas, Artur and Matthias (whence Matze). The similar sounding diminutive Azo developed from Aldelbertus with Azzo being attested since 1259 in the Lake Constance region. Alternatively, a back-formation from atzen.

August.et: Du latin Augustus (« majestueux, consacré, vénérable »).

Augusta.ete: From Latin Augusta, feminine of Augustus.

Axel.ete: From Danish Aksel, a vernacular form of Absalom.

Ayleen.ete: Rendering of English Aileen/Eileen, partly confused with Turkish Aylin.

Babsi.ete: Diminutive in -i of Barbara, compare Babs.

Barbara.ete: Borrowed from Latin Barbara, from the saint's name.

Bärbel.ete: Barb(ara) + -el, originally a hypocoristic variant of Barbara.
Bärbel.et: Diminutif de Barbara, avec le suffixe -el.

q: „Für den jetzigen Schloßherrn, der von der zweiten Frau stammte, hatte sich daraus leider kein unmittelbarer Vorteil ergeben, und Dubslav von Stechlin wäre kleiner und großer Sorgen und Verlegenheiten nie los und ledig geworden, wenn er nicht in dem benachbarten Gransee seinen alten Freund Baruch Hirschfeld gehabt hätte.“
Theodor Fontane: Der Stechlin. 2. Auflage. F. Fontane & Co., Berlin 1899 (Erstpublikation 1897, Wikisource) , Seite 9–10.

Barzilo.ete: Equivalent to German Bardilo, requiring [z] instead of [d] from Bardilo.

Basti.ete: Clipping of Bastian + -i, itself a clipping of Sebastian.

Bastienne.ete: Borrowed from French Bastienne or Clipping of Sebastienne.

q: Nach dem Tode ihres königlichen Gemahls führte Bathildis die Regentschaft für ihren minderjährigen Sohn Clothar III., regierte mit großer Weisheit und Kraft, hob die Leibeigenschaft auf, bewahrte den Frieden, stiftete viele Klöster und Spitäler.

Heilige Bathildis, Königin und Klosterfrau. In: Traunsteiner Tagblatt. Nummer 4/2013, 26. Januar 2013 (Aus dem Buch: »Illustrierte Heiligen-Legende für Schule und Haus«, erschienen im Jahre 1890, Online, abgerufen am 7. Dezember 2020) .

Benedikt.ete: Borrowed from Late Latin Benedictus, from Latin benedictus (“blessed”), perfect passive participle of benedīcō (“to speak well of, bless, praise”), from bene (“well”) + dīcō (“to speak”).

Benjamin.et: De l’hébreu ancien בנימין, Binyāmîn (« fils de la droite »).

Benno.ete: Short form of compound names that begin or end with the Germanic element bern, "bear", such as Bernhard.

Bernd.ete: Diminutive of Bernhard. The “anon” sense comes from the popular German imageboard Krautchan, where anonymous posters were known as Bernds.

Bernhard.ete: From Old High German Bernhart, from Old High German bero (“bear”, cf. Bär), + Old High German hart (“hard, strong”, cf. hart). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Bernuharduz.
Bernhard.et: Du vieux haut-allemand bero (« ours ») et de harti (« dur »).

Bernhardt.ete: From Middle High German Bernhart, from Old High German Bernhart, from Proto-West Germanic *Bernuhardu, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Bernuharduz. Equivalent to Old High German bero (“bear”) (modern Bär) + hart (“hard, strong”) (modern hart).

Bernhart.ete: From Old High German Bernhart, from Old High German bero (“bear”, cf. Bär), + Old High German hart (“hard, strong”, cf. hart). Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Bernuharduz.

Berthold.et: Du gotique *berth (« clair, brillant » → voir Bertha et Bertram) et walten (« diriger » → voir Walter).

Bertmar.ete: From Old High German Berchtmar, from Proto-Germanic *Berhtamēraz, from *berhtaz (“bright, shining”) + *mēraz (“great, famous”).

Bimbo.ete: Uncertain. The proper noun already occurs in the 19th century, and already as a name for a black person.

Bismarck.ete: Uncertain. Probably from the German town of Bismark, a compound of Biese (name of a nearby river, related to Dutch bies (“bulrush”)) and Mark (“border region”).

Björn.ete: Borrowed from Swedish Björn in the 1930s.

Bodo.ete: Either via Old Saxon bodo (“master”) or from Old High German boto (“messenger”); also a short form for given names beginning with Bodo- (Bodowin, Bodomar) or ending with -bod (as Adalbod)

Broder.et: Du bas allemand, apparenté au danois broder, à Bruder en allemand.

Bruder.et: Du vieux haut allemand bruoder, de l’indo-européen commun *bʰréh₂tēr dont sont issus brother, en anglais, брат en russe, bratr en tchèque, et frater en latin qui a donné frère en français.

Brunhilde.ete: From Middle High German Briunhilde, from Old High German *Brunnīhilta, from Proto-West Germanic *Brunnjuhildi, from Proto-Germanic *Brunjōhildiz, from *brunjǭ (“breastplate”) + *hildiz (“battle, fight”).

Burghard.ete: From Old High German burg (“castle, fortress”) + hart (“hard”).

Burghardt.ete: From Old High German burg (“castle, fortress”) + hart (“hard”).

Burkhard.ete: From Old High German burg (“castle, fortress”) + hart (“hard”).

Burkhardt.ete: From Old High German burg (“castle, fortress”) + hart (“hard”).
Burkhardt.et: Composé de Burg et de hart.

Burkhart.ete: From Old High German burg (“castle, fortress”) + hart (“hard”).

Cäsar.ete: From Latin Caesar. Doublet of Kaiser and Zar.

Celian.et: Du prénom latin Caelius, apparenté au mot caelum (« ciel »).

Celina.ete: Variant of Celine, from French Céline, ultimately from Latin.

Celine.ete: Borrowed from French Céline in the 20th century.

Charlotte.ete: Borrowed from French Charlotte and charlotte.

Christa.ete: Short form of Christiane and Christina. Popularized through 19th century German literature.

Christopher.ete: From English Christopher, as a variant of the standard German Christoph.

q: „Sie sollen sehen, daß mir in Clara und in dir noch große Freude geblieben ist und daß ich weder so schwach noch so alt bin, mich von einem Unglück niederwerfen zu lassen.“
Fanny Lewald: Jenny. In: Dieselbe (Herausgeber): Gesammelte Werke. 9. Band, Berlin 1872, Seite 237 (Zitiert nach www.zeno.org) .

„Hierdurch bestätigt sich die, von Cläre von Glümer in ihrer geistvollen Lebensbeschreibung der Schröder-Devrient gegebene Nachricht über dieß Benefiz, das von andrer Seite her in Abrede gestellt wurde.“
Max Maria von Weber: Carl Maria von Weber. Ein Lebensbild. 2. Band, Ernst Keil, Leipzig 1866, Seite 424, Fußnote 2 (Zitiert nach zeno.org) .

Cordula.ete: From Late Latin Cordula, name of a companion of Saint Ursula, associated with Latin cor (“heart”) (genitive singular cordis).

Crescentia.ete: From Latin Crēscentia, from crēscēns (“growing, increasing, rising, thriving”), from crēscō (“I grow, increase, rise, thrive”).

Detlef.ete: Low German name from Old Saxon thiad (“people”) + leva (“heir”).

Dieter.ete: From Old High German thiot (“people”) + heri (“army”).

Dietlinde.ete: From Old High German thiot (“people”) + lind (“soft, tender”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”) + Proto-Germanic *linþaz (“mild”).

Dietmar.ete: From Old High German Diotmar, from Proto-West Germanic *Þeudumārī, from Proto-Germanic *Þeudōmēraz, equivalent to Old High German diot (“people”) + mari (“fame”).

Dietrich.ete: Inherited from Middle High German Dietrich, from Old High German Diotrih, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Þeudōrīks. By surface analysis, Diet + -rich.

Dominik.ete: From Late Latin Dominicus, derived from Dominus (“Lord”).Doublet of Dominikus.

Dominikus.ete: From Late Latin Dominicus, from Latin dominicus (“pertaining to the Lord”).

Doreen.ete: From English Doreen with a spelling pronunciation.

Eberhard.ete: From Eber + hart; cognate to English Everett.

Edda.et: Abréviation de prénoms féminins en Ed- comme Edwina.

Edith.ete: Borrowed from English Edith in the 19th century.

Eduard.ete: Old English Ēadweardbor. Old French Edwardder. Middle French Edouardder. French Édouardbor. German Eduard 18th century, from French Édouard, itself from English Edward.

Egon.ete: Variant of Egino, diminutive of Germanic compound names beginning with the element Egin-, from *agi (“awe”), later merged with Old High German ekka (“sharp point”) (from *aggju). Popular during the first half of the 20th century.

Ekkehard.ete: From Old High German ekka (“sharp point”) + harti (“hard”), or ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Agjōharduz.

Ellen.ete: Borrowed from English Ellen and Danish Ellen.

Elsa.et: De Elisabeth, Elisa. Prénom popularisé par Elsa von Brabant, héroïne de l’opéra de Richard Wagner Lohengrin (1850).

Emilie.ete: From French Émilie, from Latin Aemilia.

Emma.ete: Short form of compound female given names beginning with Proto-Germanic *ermana, Proto-Germanic *irmina "whole, entire".

Emmerich.ete: From a merger of two or three of the following Germanic names: 1.) *Amalarīks, from Proto-Germanic *amalą (“hard work”), cognate with English Amery, Italian Amerigo; 2.) *Ermanarīks, from *ermanaz (“great, strong, whole”); 3.) *Haimarīks, from *haimaz (“home”), cognate with German Heinrich, English Henry. The second part in all cases is Proto-Germanic *rīks (“ruler”). Compare also Hungarian Imre.

Engelbert.ete: From Old High German. The first part has absorbed the tribal name Angle, and an extended form of the god's name Ing (as in Ingela), and was in Christian times interpreted as Engel (“an angel”). The second part is beraht (“bright”). Popularized by a martyred 13th century bishop of Cologne.

Erhard.ete: From the name of a 7th/8th century German saint, from Old High German ēra (“honour”) + harti (“hard”).

Erich.ete: Variant of Erich, borrowed from English Eric or from French Éric.

Erna.ete: Short form of Ernesta and Ernestina, Latinate feminine forms of Ernst.

Ernst.et: . Du moyen haut-allemand ernst, ernest, du vieux haut allemand ernust.

Erwin.ete: From Old High German heri (“army”) + wini (“friend”). Taken to regular use from the play Erwin und Elmire (1775) by Goethe.

Estefania.ete: From Spanish Estefanía with a stress shift. Alternatively from Portuguese Estefânia, which is stressed as in German, but is nevertheless a less likely origin.

Ester.ete: From Latin Esthēr, from Ancient Greek Ἐσθήρ (Esthḗr), from Biblical Hebrew אֶסְתֵּר (ʾestēr).

Ewald.ete: From the name of two seventh century missionaries, Old High German ewa (“law”) + waltan (“to rule”).

Fabian.ete: Borrowed from Latin Fabiānus (“belonging to Fabius”).

Fabio.ete: Borrowed from Italian Fabio, Spanish Fabio and Portuguese Fábio.

Ferdinand.ete: From Spanish Ferdinando, from Proto-Germanic *fardiz (“journey”) + *nanþaz (“daring”) (from the root of *ninþaną (“to be daring”)).

Finja.ete: Modern German feminine form of Finn.

Florentin.ete: From the Medieval Latin Flōrentīnus (literally “Florentine, from Florence”), name of a saint (Antoninus of Florence), from Latin Flōrentia (“Florence”), from flōrēns (“flourishing”).

Florentina.ete: Borrowed from Late Latin Flōrentīna, name of a Visigothic saint (died c. 612 AD); also the feminine equivalent of Latin Flōrentīnus (literally “Florentine, from Florence”).

Florentine.ete: Variant of Florentina, the feminine equivalent of Florentin, from Latin Flōrentīnus.

Florian.ete: Borrowed from Latin Flōriānus, derivative of Flōrus; name of a 4th century saint, patron of Austria.

Folkwin.ete: From Middle High German *Volkewîn, from Old High German *Folkwini, from Proto-West Germanic *Folkawini, equivalent to Old High German folk (“people”) + wini (“friend”).

Frank.ete: From Middle High German Franke, from Old High German Franko (“a Frank”). Used in the Middle Ages and revived in the 19th century.

Franz.ete: Clipping of Franziskus, from Latin Franciscus, cognate to English Francis.
Franz.et: De Franziskus issu du latin Franciscus ; apparenté à Frank.

Frauke.ete: From a German Low German [Term?] diminutive of uncertain origin, possibly related to Frau, and by folk etymology interpreted as "little lady".

Frieda.ete: Short form of names containing the Germanic element fried "peace", such as Friederike or Elfriede.

Friedbert.ete: From Proto-Germanic *Friþuberhtaz, equivalent to Old High German fridu (“peace”) + beraht (“bright”).

Friedegund.ete: From Old High German fridu (“peace”) + gunda (“battle”).

Friederich.ete: Inherited from Old High German Fridurih (fridu (“peace”) + -rih (“suffix for male names, originally a noun meaning king”)), from Proto-West Germanic *Friþurīk.

Friedhelm.ete: From Old High German Friduhelm (fridu (“peace”) + helm (“helmet, protection”)).

Friedrich.ete: Inherited from Old High German Fridurih (fridu (“peace”) + -rih (“suffix for male names, originally a noun meaning king”)), from Proto-West Germanic *Friþurīk.
Friedrich.et: De Friede (« paix ») et Rick (« puissant, important » (parfois Roi)).

q: Louise ist auf dem dünnen Eis eingebrochen, heroisch eilt der junge Offizier zu ihrer Rettung. Der Erzähler gesteht den deutschen Soldaten, die schnell Louisens und Fritzens Rettung organisieren, Entschlossenheit und Tatkraft zu.

Julia Schroda, Nationaler Anspruch und regionale Identität im Reichsland Elsaß-Lothringen im Spiegel des französisch-sprachigen Elsaßromans (1871-1914), Inaugural-Dissertation zur Erlangung der Doktorwürde der Philogischen Fakultät der Albert-Ludwigs-Universität Freiburg i. Br., (2008, ISBN 978-3-03911-460-3), Seite 287
Fritz.ete: Shortened form of Friedrich. Cognate to English Fred.

Fulko.et: Apparenté à Volk (« peuple ») et au prénom Volker.

Gabriel.ete: From Latin Gabriel, from Koine Greek Γαβρῑήλ (Gabrīḗl), from Biblical Hebrew גַּבְרִיאֵל (gaḇrīʾḗl)

Genoveva.ete: From Medieval Latin Genovefa, Genoveva, possibly either of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *kunją (“kin, family”) + *wībą (“woman, wife”), or of Celtic origin, ultimately from Proto-Celtic *genos (“family, clan”). Popularized by a 17th century romance of Genoveva of Brabant.

Georg.et: Du latin Georgius, dérivé du grec ancien Γεώργιος, Geórgios.

Gerda.ete: From modern Scandinavian Gerda, from Old Norse Gerðr. By folk etymology sometimes interpreted as a female form of German Gerd or as a variant of Gertrud.

Gereon.ete: Ripuarian short form of Latin Hieronymus, from Ancient Greek Ἱερώνυμος (Hierṓnumos, “holy name”). Compare Dutch Jeroen and Italian Geronimo.

Gerhard.ete: Inherited from Old High German Gērhart, from Proto-West Germanic *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *hard(ī) (“brave, hard”). Cognates include French Gérard, Old English Gārheard, Dutch Gerard, and Geert.
Gerhard.et: Du haut-allemand ger (« lance ») et hard (« dur »).

Gerhardt.ete: Inherited from Old High German Gērhart, from Proto-West Germanic *Gaiʀahard, from *gaiʀ (“spear”) + *hard(ī) (“brave, hard”). Cognates include French Gérard, Old English Gārheard, Dutch Gerard, and Geert. Compare Gearheart, Gearhart, Garhart.

Gerlach.ete: From Proto-Germanic; see Gerlach; possibly from Middle High German.

Gerlinde.ete: From Old High German ger (“spear”) + lind (“soft, tender”).

Germund.ete: From the Old High German equivalent of Old Norse Geirmundr, meaning "spear" + "protection".

Gertrud.ete: From Old High German gēr (“spear”) + Proto-Germanic *þrūþiz (“strength”) or Proto-Germanic *trut (“maiden”).

Gesine.ete: Elaborated form of Gesa, from a German Low German diminutive of Gertrud.

Giselbrecht.ete: From Old High German, from gisil (“hostage”) + berht (“bright, illustrious”).

Gottfried.et: → voir Gott et Friede : « paix de Dieu ».

Gotthard.ete: Name of a 10th - 11th century German saint, from Old High German got (“God”) + harti, herti (“hard, strong”). Cognate with English Goddard.

Gottlieb.ete: Old High German got (“God”) + Old High German leiba (“descendant, son”). Used by Pietists as a translation of Amadeus and Theophil through the folk etymology Gott + lieb (“beloved”).
Gottlieb.et: Composé de Gott (« dieu ») et de lieben (« aimer »), en équivalent de Amadeus.

Gottschalk.ete: From Old High German Godescalc, from got (“God”) and skalk (“servant”).
Gottschalk.et: Avec le sens de « serviteur de Dieu », composé de Gott et du gotique skalk qui donne Schalk en allemand moderne, scalco en italien, voir mareschal en ancien français.

Gunda.ete: Short form of compound given names containing the Old High German element gund (“battle”).

Günther.ete: A medieval variant of Gunther, from Old High German gund (“battle”) + heri (“army”), from Proto-West Germanic *Gunþihari, from Proto-Germanic *Gunþiharjaz.
Günther.et: Du vieux haut allemand → voir Gonthier.

Gunthild.ete: From Old High German gund (“battle”) + hilt (“battle”).

Hagen.et: Du vieux norrois et apparenté à l’islandais Högni.

Hajo.ete: Short form of Hans-Joachim or Hans-Josef.

Hannah.et: De l’hébreu חַנָה, Ḥanah, issu de חַן ḥan (« grâce », « charme »).

Hans.ete: A medieval short form of Johannes (“John”).
Hans.et: Abréviation de Johannes. Attesté depuis le Moyen-Age.

q: Hänschen sah betroffen in das plötzlich umwölkte Gesicht des Alten und verschwand mit seiner Schultasche unter dem Eingang.

Conrad von Bolanden: Die Schwarzen und die Rothen. Erster Theil. In: Projekt Gutenberg-DE. Friedrich Pustet, 1873, Im alten Hause (URL, abgerufen am 7. Januar 2021) . Alte Version im Internet-Archiv abrufbar. *
Hänschen.et: Mot dérivé de Hans (« Jean »), avec le suffixe -chen.

Hartmut.ete: From Old High German harti, herti (“hard, strong”) + muot (“spirit”).

Hedwig.ete: From Old High German Haduwig, Hadwig, from Proto-Germanic *Haþuwīgą, from *haþuz (“fight”) + *wīgą (“battle”).
Hedwig.et: Du vieux haut allemand Haduwig, Hadwig, du proto-germanique occidental *Haþuwīg, du proto-germanique *Haþuwīgą, de *haþuz (« combat, dispute ») + *wīgą (« bataille »).

Heidi.ete: Originally a Swiss German diminutive of Adelheid + -i

Hein.ete: From an earlier form Henn, from Middle High German hein, since the 14th century.

Heinrich.ete: From Old High German Heimrih, Haimirich (8th century), composed of heim (“home”) + -rih (“suffix for male names, originally a noun meaning king”); corresponds to Proto-West Germanic *Haimarīk, from Proto-Germanic *Haimarīks. Cognate to English Henry (via French Henri), Dutch Hendrik, Danish Henrik.
Heinrich.et: Anciennement Heimerich, de *haim, en allemand moderne Heim (« maison »), *rik, en allemand moderne Reich (« empire »).

Helene.et: Du latin Helena, emprunté au grec ancien Ἑλένη, Helénê.

Helle.ete: Short form with hypocoristic -e. Compare Kalle, Matze, etc.

Helmut.ete: Probably from Proto-Germanic *helmaz and *mōdaz, but derivations from MHG heil/helm + muot have also been suggested. The name is shaped similar to modern German hell + Mut ("clear courage").

Hendrik.ete: Borrowed from Dutch Hendrik, as a variant of the standard German Heinrich.

Herbert.ete: From Old High German Heriberaht, from Proto-West Germanic *Hariberht. Modern cognates include English Herbert and English Hebbard, Czech Herbert, French Herbert and Swedish Herbert

Heribert.ete: From Old High German [Term?]. Doublet of Herbert, via French.

Hermann.ete: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *harjaz + *mann- and corresponding to the common noun *harjamann- (“warrior”); equivalent to Heer (“army”) + Mann (“man”).
Hermann.et: Du gotique herman (« guerrier ») → voir Heer et Mann.

Hermine.ete: A nineteenth century feminine form of Hermann.

Hertha.ete: Invented in 19th-century Germany from a misreading of Nerthus, name of a goddess in Germania (98 BCE) by Roman senator Tacitus. Nerthus is a Latinized form from a Proto-Germanic *Nerþuz, apparently cognate to Old Norse Njǫrðr.
Hertha.et: Corruption du latin Nerthus par rapprochement avec Erde (« Terre »), earth en anglais. Le mot fait Njörðr en vieux norrois, Njörður en islandais, Njord en suédois.

Hildebrand.ete: From Old High German Hiltibrant, from Proto-Germanic *Hildibrandaz.

Hildebrandt.ete: From Old High German Hiltibrant, from Proto-Germanic *Hildibrandaz.

Hildebrant.ete: From Old High German Hiltibrant, from Proto-Germanic *Hildibrandaz.

Hildegard.ete: Ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Hildigardu, from Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle”) + *gardaz (“enclosure”), with the approximate meaning “battle protector”. The modern form is of West Germanic but not High German origin, as it does not show the characteristic High German shift of *d to t. Compare Old High German Hildigard, Hiltigart.
Hildegard.et: Du vieux haut allemand.Composé de hiltja (« combat ») et de gard (« abri »)

Horst.ete: Uncertain. Possibly related to the common noun (etymology 1). First used in an 18th-century play, taken into regular use in the 19th century, popular after 1920, now rare for a child. Compare etymology 3.
Horst.et: Du vieux haut allemand hurst, apparenté à hurst (« broussaille ») en anglais, horst (« broussaille, nid d’oiseau ») en néerlandais, chrást (« touffe de feuilles ») en tchèque, хворост, khvórost (« broussaille, bois mort ») en russe.

Ida.ete: Name of early female saints, shortened from compound given names beginning with Germanic element Ida-, Idu-. The meaning is debated, possibly cognate with the Old Norse ið (“work”), or related to the goddess Iðunn. Since its revival in the 19th century also used as a diminutive of Adelaide.

Ignaz.ete: From Ignatius by dropping the Latin ending.

Immanuel.ete: From Hebrew עִמָּנוּאֵל (imanu'él), from עִמָּנוּ אֵל (imánu él, literally “God is with us”).

Ingeborg.ete: From Norwegian, Swedish and Danish Ingeborg in the 19th century.

Ingo.ete: Pet form of names in Ing-, chiefly Ingolf.
Ingo.et: De même radical que le latin Ingaevones (« peuple germain de la Baltique »), Ingauni (« peuple ligurien »), au norrois Yngvi.

Ingrid.ete: From Swedish, Norwegian and Danish Ingrid, from Old Norse Ingiríðr.

Irma.ete: Short form of female compound given names beginning with the Germanic element irm(en)-, erm(en) "whole, entire". Made popular through nineteenth century German fiction.

Irmgard.ete: Name of an 11th century German saint, from Old High German *irmin + gard (“enclosure, protection”).

Isaak.ete: Borrowed from Latin Isaāc, from Ancient Greek Ἰσαᾱ́κ (Isaā́k), from Biblical Hebrew יִצְחָק (Yiṣḥāq, literally “he laughs”).

Jakob.ete: Inherited from Middle High German Jācob. Doublet of Jakobus, which comes directly from Latin.

Jan.ete: From Central and Low German dialects. Modern use may have been reinforced by related Germanic and Slavic forms.

Jana.ete: Today usually interpreted as the feminine form of Jan, though it can also derive from Juliana.

Jannek.ete: Affectionated form of Jann. Originated in the 1990s.

Jasmin.ete: 16th century, from French jasmin, from Spanish jazmín, from Arabic ياسَمِين (yāsamīn), from Persian یاسمن (yâsaman). The pronunciation is spelling-based and thus only coincidentally very close to the Middle Eastern etyma. Use as a personal name following wider European usage since the 19th century.

Jelena.ete: Borrowed from Russian Еле́на (Jeléna), from Latin Helena, from Ancient Greek Ἑλένη (Helénē). Doublet of Helene.

Jennifer.ete: From English Jennifer in the 20th century.
Jennifer.et: De l’anglais Jennifer, issu du gallois Gwenhwyfar, équivalent de Guenièvre.

Jessica.ete: Borrowed from English Jessica, popular at the end of the 20th century.

Joachim.ete: Borrowed from Latin Iōāchīmus, from Ancient Greek Ἰωακείμ (Iōakeím), Ἰωακίμ (Iōakím) (2 Kings 24), from Biblical Hebrew יְהוֹיָקִים (yəhôyâqîm, literally “may Yahweh raise up”).

Johanna.ete: From Latin Iohanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα (Iōánna), which see.

Johannes.ete: From Medieval Latin Jōhannēs, from Late Latin Iōhannēs, variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān) (perhaps from a former J^əhôħānān). Cognate with English John.

q: „Pia, du weißt ja, dass ich nichts dagegen habe, wenn du deine Freunde zu Besuch hast, aber jetzt möchte ich doch wenigstens mal bei Jorindes Eltern anrufen und fragen, ob das so in Ordnung für sie ist.“
Martha Sophie Marcus: Elsternseele. Baumhaus Verlag/Digital Lübbe in der Bastei Lübbe GmbH & Co. KG, Köln 2011, ISBN 978-3-8387-1151-5, Seite ‹ohne Seitenangabe› (E-Book; zitiert nach Google Books) .

Joscha.ete: Germanized spelling of Hungarian Józsa, itself an affectionate form of József.

Joschka.ete: Borrowed from Hungarian Jóska, a diminutive of József.

Josef.ete: Latin Josephus and/or Ancient Greek Ἰωσήφ (Iōsḗph)

Judas.ete: From Latin Judas, from Ancient Greek Ἰούδας (Ioúdas), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏā).

Judith.ete: From Latin Judith, from Hebrew יְהוּדִית (yəhūḏīṯ, “woman from Judea, Jewess”).

Jupp.ete: Pet form of Josef, Joseph. Regarding the final -p one might suspect influence by Jakob, but the southern German equivalent Sepp seems to imply that the name was formerly pronounced with a final /p/, rather than /f/. At any rate, Jupp is now associated exclusively with Josef. Compare also Dutch Joop.

Jürgen.ete: Derived from Low German, from Middle Low German Jurian (compare Dutch Jurriaan, Swedish Örjan), from Latin Geōrgius (which see for cognates), from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios), whence also Georg, Jörg.

Justus.ete: Borrowed from Latin Iustus, also used as a Latinization of Jost.

Jutta.ete: Perhaps from a Middle Low German diminutive of Judith, from Hebrew יְהוּדִית (yəhūḏīṯ, “Judith”). A Germanic origin has also been suggested. Compare Danish Jytte.

Kai.ete: Taken into regular use in the 20th century; either borrowed from Danish Kaj, or from a West Frisian baby talk form of Kaimbe, Kempe (“fighter, warrior”), Gerrit (“Gerard”), Cornelis (“Cornelius”) and Kleis (“Nicholas”).

Kajetan.ete: From the Latin Caiētānus (“inhabitant of Gaeta”), re-Latinized from Italian Gaetano, name of a saint.

Kalle.ete: As a nickname probably a native variant of Karl. As an actual given name, however, reinforced by Swedish Kalle through Kalle Blomquist (Swedish Kalle Blomkvist, English Bill Bergson).

Karl.ete: From Old High German karal, from Proto-Germanic *karlaz (“free man”), *karilaz (“man, elder”). Cognate with French and English Charles.
Karl.et: Du vieux haut allemand Karl dont est issu Kerl (« bonhomme »).

Kaspar.ete: Via Biblical Hebrew גִּזְבָּר (gizbar), from Classical Syriac ܓܙܒܪܐ (gēzaḇrā), from Old Persian *ganzabarah, from Old Median *ganǰabarah. Compare Bavarian Kasperl.

Kevin.ete: Borrowed from English Kevin. First popularised in the late 1970s after footballer Kevin Keegan, who played for Hamburger SV from 1977 to 1980.

Kilian.ete: Borrowed from Irish Cillian, originally in honor of an Irish seventh century missionary to Würzburg.

Kirsten.et: Du danois Kirsten ou du norvégien Kirsten, issu du latin Christiana (« chrétienne »).

Konrad.ete: From Middle High German Kuonrāt, from Old High German Kuonrad, Chuonrad, from Proto-West Germanic *Kōnirād; equivalent to Proto-West Germanic *kōnī (“bold, brave”) + *rād (“counsel”). The modern spelling with final -d has been influenced by unshifted Central German and Low German variants.
Konrad.et: Équivalent ducomposé de kühn (« audacieux ») et de Rat (« conseil »).

Kunigunde.ete: Inherited from Old High German Kunigunde.
Kunigunde.et: Du vieux haut allemand, composé de kunni (« famille, tribu, génération » → voir kunne en néerlandais) et gund (« bataille » → voir Gonthier et Radegonde).

Kurt.ete: A medieval short form of Konrad.

Laila.ete: Both from Arabic لَيْلَى (laylā) and Finnish Laila.

Larissa.ete: Borrowed from Russian Лари́са (Larísa) in the 20th century.

Lars.ete: Borrowed from Danish, Norwegian and Swedish Lars in the latter half of the 20th century.

Laurenz.ete: Borrowed from Latin Laurentius. A variant of Lorenz.

Laurin.ete: Uncertain. Name of a king of dwarfs in German folklore.

Lene.et: Aphérèse de Magdalena ou de Helena.

Lennart.ete: From Swedish and Danish Lennart. A newer variant of the German Leonhard.

Leonhard.et: Réfection sur le latin leo (« lion »), de *lewehart → voir Löwe et Härte.

Leopold.et: D’origine germanique composé de leod (« peuple ») et bald (« courageux »).

Lieselotte.ete: Liese + Lotte, shortened from Elisabeth + Charlotte.
Lieselotte.et: Nom combinant les prénoms Liese (diminutif de Elisabeth) et Lotte (diminutif de Charlotte).

Lina.ete: Short form of Karolina and other names ending in -lina, used as a formal given name since the 19th century.

Linda.ete: Originates as a short form of names such as Dietlinde and Sieglinde. Secondarily augmented by Spanish linda and Portuguese linda (“beautiful, pretty”).

Linus.ete: Borrowed from Latin Linus, borrowed from Ancient Greek Λῖνος (Lînos).

Liselotte.et: Dérivé du prénom féminin Lieselotte, combinant les prénoms « Elisabeth » (dont le diminutif est « Lise ») et « Charlotte » (dont le diminutif est « Lotte »).

Liutpold.et: D’origine germanique composé du vieux haut allemand liut (« peuple ») qui a donné Leute, et bald (« courageux »).

Lore.ete: * Contraction of Eleonore; see English Eleanor for more. * Clipping of Hannelore

Lothar.ete: From 9th C. Frankish Ludher, from Proto-West Germanic *Hlūdhari via Old Dutch or Old French
Lothar.et: Du vieux haut allemand hlut (« renommée ») et heri (« armée »).

Louis.ete: Borrowed from French Louis. Doublet of Ludwig.

Ludger.ete: From Old Saxon Liudigēr, from Proto-West Germanic *liudi (“men, people”) + *gaiʀ (“spear”). The modern form through Latin Lud(i)gerus after the 8th-century saint.

Ludwig.ete: From Middle High German Ludewig, from Old High German Ludhuwīg, Hludwig, *Hlūtwīg, from Proto-West Germanic *Hlūdawīg. The first element is (h)lūt (“famed; loud”) (whence modern German laut), from Proto-Germanic *hlūdaz, *hlūþaz (whence also English loud), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱlew- (“to hear”). The second element is Old High German wīg (“battle, strife”) from Proto-Germanic *wīgą. The name is attested as Ludhuwīg in the Straßburger Eide of 842 (where it contrasts with Old French Lodhuuig and Latin Lodhuuic), and as Hludwig in the Rhine Franconian Old High German of the Ludwigslied of 881 (where it contrasts with Latin Hluduicus). Compare Clovis, Dutch Lodewijk, English Lewis, and Frenc
Ludwig.et: Du gotique hlud (« illustre ») et wig (« combat »).

Luisa.ete: From Old French Louise, feminine of Louis, further traced to Latin Ludovicus. Cognate with Spanish Luisa and French Louisa.

Lukas.ete: Borrowed from Latin Lūcās and Ancient Greek Λουκᾶς (Loukâs).

Lulu.ete: From a diminutive of Luise and other female names beginning with Lu-.

Lutz.et: Du diminutif de Ludwig ou de Ludger.

Madeleine.ete: Borrowed from French Madeleine. Doublet of Magdalena.

Magdalena.ete: From Ancient Greek Μαγδαληνή (Magdalēnḗ, “woman from Magdala”).

Manfred.ete: Literally, “Human-peace” (perhaps as opposed to divine peace); from Old High German man (“man”; “human”) + fridu (“peace”). Best known for a 13th century king of Sicily, made famous by literature, as in Byron's poem Manfred (1816–1817). Revived in the 19th century.

Manuel.et: De l’hébreu עִמָּנוּאֵל (imanou El), signifiant « Dieu est avec nous ».

Marc.ete: From Middle High German marke, from Old High German marka, from Proto-West Germanic *marku, cognate with Latin margo, whence English margin.

Margit.ete: From Hungarian, Norwegian and Swedish Margit.

Maria.ete: From Vulgate Latin Maria, from Ancient Greek Μαρία (María), Μαριάμ (Mariám), from Aramaic מרים (Maryām), corresponding to the Hebrew מרים (Miryām).

Marian.ete: Borrowed from Latin Marianus, derivative of Marius.

Marie.ete: Variant of Maria, or borrowed from French Marie.

Marie-Theres.ete: From Marie + Therese, in imitation of French Marie-Thérèse. Popularized by European royalty, for example an 18th century Queen of Austria.

Marina.ete: From Latin Marīna, feminine of Marīnus.

Marlene.ete: Combination of Maria and Lene (from Helene or Magdalene). Best known for the actress Marlene Dietrich, baptized Maria Magdalene.
Marlene.et: Mot-valise formé à partir de Maria et de Lene.

Martin.ete: From Latin Mārtīnus (“of or like Mars” or “little Mars”), Mārs, Mārtis + -īnus (diminutive suffix).

Marvin.ete: Borrowed from English Marvin in the 20th century.

Marwig.ete: From Old High German Mārwīg, from Proto-West Germanic *Mārīwīg. Cognate with Latin Meroveus.

Matthäus.ete: Borrowed from Latin Matthaeus, from Ancient Greek Ματθαῖος (Matthaîos), from Aramaic מַתַּי (mattay).

Matthias.ete: Borrowed from Latin Matthias. Related to Matthäus.

Maximilian.ete: Saint's name from Latin Maximilianus, a derivative of Maximus "the greatest". It was used in German royal houses after Friedrich III chose it for his son in 1459, explaining it as a combination of the names of two Roman generals, Maximus and Aemilianus.

Mechthild.ete: From Old High German Mehthilt, from Proto-Germanic *Mahtihildiz.

Mehdi.ete: Chiefly used by Iranian immigrants, from Persian مهدی (mahdi), from Arabic مَهْدِيّ (mahdiyy, “rightly guided”). Compare Mahdi.

Melanie.ete: Borrowed from Latin Melania, from Ancient Greek μέλας (mélas, “black, dark”).

Melina.ete: Can be construed as a short form of names like Amelina (Ameline) and Carmelina (Carmela). The modern German usage derives mainly from Greek Μελίνα (Melína), stage name of the Greek actress Melina Mercouri, born Μαρία Αμαλία (María Amalía).

Mendel.et: Du yiddish מענדל, mendl, diminutif de Menachem

Merle.ete: Borrowed from English Merle with a spelling pronunciation (likely reinforced by etymology 1 above).

Merlin.et: : Des langues celtiques mori-dunon (« forteresse de la mer »).

Micha.ete: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָה (mīḵāh), whence also English Micah; see there for more information.

Michäas.ete: Borrowed from Latin Michaeās, from Ancient Greek Μῐχαίᾱς (Mĭkhaíās), from Biblical Hebrew מִיכָה (mīḵāh), shortened form of מִיכַיְהוּ (mīḵāyᵊhū, “who is like Yahweh”).

Michael.ete: From Vulgate Latin Michaēl, Michahēl, from Biblical Hebrew מיכאל (mikhael, literally “who is like God?”).

Michaela.ete: Feminine form of Michael taken into general use in the 20th century.

Michel.ete: Popular form of Michael with reduction of unstressed syllables.

Milan.ete: From Czech Milan, Slovene Milan, etc.

Minna.ete: Popularized by the comedy Minna von Barnhelm (1767) by G. E. Lessing, see quotations.

q: „Dein Vater ging unter und Momme, mein Sohn.“
Otto Ernst: Nis Randert. Gedicht von 1907.

Moritz.ete: From Middle High German [Term?], from Latin Mauritius, from the 3rd-century Egyptian Saint. Though Christian in origin, Moritz was a name typical of assimilating Jews in the 19th and earlier 20th centuries. These probably used it as a loose Germanisation of such names as Moses or Mordechai. The name has gained new popularity in Germany since the late 20th century.

Natascha.et: Emprunt au russe Наташа, Natáša, diminutif de Наталия, Natálija.

q: „Da Naz, a niederösterreichischer Baurnbui, geht in d’Fremd.“
Joseph Misson: Da Naz, a niederösterreichischer Baurnbui, geht in d’Fremd.. Gedicht in unterennsischer Mundart. Wien 1850

Nazi.et: Forme abrégée et hypocoristique de Ignatius.

Neidhart.et: Composé de Neid (« envie ») et de hart.

Nele.ete: A German Low German [Term?] pet form of Cornelia.

Nena.ete: Popularized by the singer Nena, from Spanish nena (“girl”).

Nico.ete: Nickname for Nikolaus, with formal given name status since the 20th century.

Nikolaus.ete: Borrowed from Latin Nīcolāus. Compare English Nicholas.
Nikolaus.et: Du latin Nicolaus, issu du grec ancien Νικόλαος, Nikólaos.

Norbert.et: De Nord (« nord ») et *berht (« brillant, illustre »).

Oda.ete: Short form of female compound names beginning with the Germanic element ot "riches"; cognate with Old Norse Auðr (whence Icelandic Auður and Faroese Eyð/Eyður).

Ole.ete: Borrowed from Norwegian and Danish Ole.

Olga.ete: Derived from Russian and Ukrainian О́льга (Ólʹha) in the 19th century.

Oskar.ete: Borrowed from English Oscar, from Middle Irish Oscar.

Otto.ete: Short form of Old High German compound names beginning with the element ōt (“riches”), such as Ottokar and Otmar, from Proto-West Germanic *aud, from Proto-Germanic *audaz (“treasure”). Name of a 10th century German emperor.
Otto.et: Du vieux haut allemand ot (« propriété », « patrimoine »).

Ottomar.ete: From Old High German Audomar, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Audamār, from a compound of Proto-Germanic *audaz (“treasure”) and *mērijaz (“famous”). Compare French Omer.

Otwin.ete: From Old High German Audowin, from Proto-West Germanic *Audawini, from Proto-Germanic *Audawiniz, from *audaz (“wealth, riches”) + *winiz (“friend”). Cognate with English Edwin, Faroese Eyðun, Icelandic Auðunn, Norwegian Nynorsk Audun, and Swedish Öden.

Patrizia.ete: Borrowed from Italian Patrizia, or a spelling variant of Patricia.

Per.ete: From Swedish, Norwegian and Danish Per in the 19th century.

Peter.ete: Borrowed from Latin Petrus, from Ancient Greek Πέτρος (Pétros), from πέτρος (pétros, “stone, rock”), related to πέτρα (pétra).
Peter.et: Du latin Petrus, dérivé du grec ancien Πέτρος, Pétros.

Philipp.ete: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Φίλιππος (Phílippos, “fond of horses”), from φιλέω (philéō, “I like”) + ἵππος (híppos, “horse”).
Philipp.et: Du latin Philippus, lui-même du grec ancien Φίλιππος, Phílippos (« qui aime les chevaux »).

Raban.et: Du vieux haut allemand raban (« corbeau »).

Rainer.ete: From Old High German *Reginheri, from Proto-Germanic *Raginaharjaz, from Proto-Germanic *raginą (“counsel by the gods”) + *harjaz (“army”). Cognate to English Rayner, Danish Regner, Faroese, Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish Ragnar.

Ralf.ete: Borrowed from English Ralph in the nineteenth century.

Raphael.ete: From Latin Raphael, from Hebrew רָפָאֵל (Rāfāʾēl).

Reiner.ete: From Old High German Reginheri, from Proto-Germanic *Raginaharjaz, from Proto-Germanic *raginą (“counsel by the gods”) + *harjaz (“army”). Cognate with English Rayner, Danish Regner, Faroese, Icelandic, Norwegian, and Swedish Ragnar.

Reinhard.ete: From Middle High German Reinhart, from Old High German Reginhart (also Raginhart), from Proto-Germanic *Raginaharduz, a compound of *raginą and *harduz. Cognate with English Reynard. Doublet of Reineke. Compare also Gotthard.

Reinhart.ete: From Middle High German Reinhart, from Old High German Reginhart (also Raginhart), from Proto-Germanic *Raginaharduz, a compound of *raginą and *harduz. Cognate with English Reynard. Doublet of Reineke.

Reinhold.ete: From Old High German Raginald, from Proto-Germanic *Raginawaldaz; see there for cognates and further etymology. The replacement of earlier -old by -hold is secondary and probably due to association with the Middle High German holt (“friendly, loyal”). The first element, originally ragin-/regin-, may now be identified with rein (“pure”) through folk etymology. This name was popularised by various heroic figures of medieval legend, particularly from the Dietrich von Bern cycle, such as Reinhold von Montalban (The Four Sons of Aymon), Reinhold von Meilan (The Dietrich Saga), and Saint Reinhold von Köln.

Renata.et: Du latin renata, du participe parfait passif féminin du verbe renasci. Signifie : la renaissance.

Renate.et: Du latin renata, du participe parfait passif féminin du verbe renasci. Signifie : la renaissance.

Richard.et: Du vieux haut allemand *Ricohard → voir reich et hart.

Rita.ete: From Italian Rita at the end of the 19th century.

Robert.ete: From Middle High German Robert, from Latin Robertus, from Frankish, from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþiberhtaz. Reinforced since the 18th century by French Robert. Other (chiefly southern) German forms are Rupert and Ruprecht.

Roland.ete: From Middle High German Ruolant, Ruoland, from Old High German Hruotland, *Hrōdlant, from Proto-West Germanic *Hrōþiland, from *hrōþi (“praise, fame”) + *land (“land”).

Rolf.ete: Medieval German contraction of Rudolf. Later associated with modern Scandinavian Rolf.

Rose.ete: Inherited from Middle High German rôse, from Old High German rōsa, from Latin rosa.

Roswitha.ete: From the Germanic elements Proto-Germanic *hrōþiz (“fame”) and *swinþaz (“strong”), via Old Saxon as evidenced by the loss of -n-.

Rüdiger.ete: From Middle High German Rüedeger, from Old High German Ruodigēr, from Proto-West Germanic *Hrōþigaiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþigaizaz. Cognate with English Hrothgar and Roger.

Rudolf.ete: From Middle High German Rudolf, from Old High German Ruodolf, from Proto-West Germanic *Hrōþiwulf.
Rudolf.et: Du proto-germanique *Hrōþiwulfaz composé de hrod « gloire » et wulf « loup ».

Rupert.ete: From the Middle High German Ruoperht, from Old High German Hruodperht, from Proto-West Germanic *Hrōþiberht, from Proto-Germanic *Hrōþiberhtaz.

Sabine.ete: From the Latin saint's name Sabina.

Samantha.ete: Borrowed from English Samantha in the 1960s.

Sascha.ete: From Russian Са́ша (Sáša, “Sasha”), a pet form of Алекса́ндра (Aleksándra, “Alexandra”) or Алекса́ндр (Aleksándr, “Alexander”).

Saskia.ete: Borrowed from Dutch Saskia in the 20th century.

Scheherazade.ete: Borrowed from Russian Шехераза́да (Šexerazáda), from Persian شهرازاد (šahrâzâd), alternative form of شهرزاد (šahrzâd, literally “child of the city”), from شهر (šahr, “city”) + ـزاد (-zâd, “child of”). The noun is a reference to the fictional character.

Schurl.ete: Borrowed from Bavarian Schurl, possibly from French Georges, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios).

Schurli.ete: Borrowed from Bavarian Schurli, possibly from French Georges, from Latin Geōrgius, from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios).

Seibert.ete: From Old High German Sigbert, from Proto-West Germanic *Sigiberht, from *sigi (“victory”) (whence Sieg) + *berht (“bright”).

Selina.ete: A variant spelling of Celina, of Latin [Term?] origin.

Sergej.et: Transcription du prénom russe Сергей. → voir Serge

Sibylle.ete: Latin Sibylla, from Ancient Greek Σίβυλλα (Síbulla).

Siegbert.ete: From Old High German Sigbert, from Proto-West Germanic *Sigiberht, from *sigi (“victory”) (whence Sieg) + *berht (“bright”).

Siegert.ete: A variant of Sieghart with loss of the h and weakening of the secondary syllable vowel. From Old High German sigu + Old High German harti.

Siegfried.ete: From Middle High German Sîfrit, from Old High German Sigifrid, from Proto-West Germanic *Sigifriþu, from Proto-Germanic *Sigifriþuz.
Siegfried.et: Composé de Sieg (« victoire ») et de Frieden (« paix »).

Sieghard.ete: From Old High German sigu + Old High German harti.

Sieghardt.ete: From Old High German sigu + Old High German harti.

Sieghart.ete: Inherited from Middle High German Sighart, Old High German Sigihart, from sigu (“victory”) + harti (“hardness”).

Sieghold.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + Old High German walt (“power, authority”).

Siegholt.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + Old High German walt (“power, authority”).

Sieglinde.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + lind (“soft, tender”).

Siegmund.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + munt (“protection”), and ultimately from Proto-Germanic *Sigimunduz; cognate with Norwegian Sigmund. The father of Siegfried in the Nibelungenlied.

Siegwald.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + Old High German walt (“power, authority”).

Siegwaldt.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + Old High German walt (“power, authority”).

Siegwolf.ete: From Old High German sigu (“victory”) + Old High German wolf (“wolf”).

Sigmund.et: De Sigu : signifiant « victoire », et Mund ou Munt, signifiant « bouche » ou « protection » (« protecteur victorieux » ou « celui qui vainc par la parole »).

Sigrid.ete: Borrowed from Danish, Norwegian and Swedish Sigrid, ultimately from Old Norse Sigríðr.

Sina.ete: Short form of names ending in -sina, such as Rosina or Teresina.

Sophie.et: Du grec ancien σοφία, sophía (« savoir »).

Steffen.ete: Popular form with reduction of the unstressed syllable.

Susanne.ete: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Σουσάννα (Sousánna), the New Testament form of Hebrew שׁוֹשַׁנָּה (šōšannā, “lily”).

Svenja.ete: Modern German feminine form of Sven.

Taleiothe.ete: From an Old High German compound name, from the elements talo + -joto.

Tanja.ete: From Russian Таня (Tanja), diminutive of Татьяна (Tatʹjana), whence less common German Tatjana. Compare English Tania, Tanya, Tatiana.

Tatjana.ete: Borrowed from Russian Татья́на (Tatʹjána), from Latin Tatiana. Cognate to English Tatiana.

Theres.ete: A phonetic rendering of French Thérèse (“Theresa”).

Thorsten.ete: From Danish Torsten, from Old Norse Þorsteinn, the root of English Thurstan, from Þórr (“Thor”) + steinn (“stone”).

Till.ete: Medieval diminutive of compound given names beginning with Diet- (such as Dieter or Dietrich), from Old High German thoit (“people”).
Till.et: Diminutif des prénoms en Diet- → voir Dieter, Dietmar et Dietrich.

Tillmann.ete: Combination of the given name Till and the ending -mann, in analogy with old names like Hermann and Hartmann.
Tillmann.et: Composé de Till et de Mann.

Tim.ete: Originally a diminutive of Timotheus and Dietmar.

Traute.ete: Short form of names ending in -traut, -traud, such as Waltraud or Gertraud.

Ulrich.ete: Inherited from Old High German Uodalrich (Odalric, Udalric), from uodal (“heritage, homestead”) + rihhi (“ruler”). English sources also suggest Old English wulf (“wolf”) + ric (“ruler”).

Ursel.ete: From Middle High German Ursele, popular form of Latin Ursula with native treatment of unstressed syllables.

Ursula.ete: Learned borrowing from Latin Ursula. Compare the popular form Ursel, from Middle High German Ursele.

Uschi.ete: Diminutive in -i of Uschel, Urschel, dialectal pronunciations of Ursel, Germanised form of Ursula.

Ute.ete: Inherited from Middle High German Uote. High German variant of Oda, short form of names beginning with Germanic ot (“riches”); name of a queen in the Nibelungenlied.

Uwe.ete: A Frisian name of debated origin; possibly a short form of Germanic compound names beginning with *ob- "industrious" or Old High German agil- (“sword”) (etymologically allied with Latin acūtus, Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”)). The Scandinavian variant Ove may have Old Norse origin.

Valentin.ete: From Latin Valentinus. The name was already borrowed in Old High German and therefore shows dialectal forms with umlaut and contraction (cf. Luxembourgish Välten, whence Vältesdag); but in learned parlance it was continuously relatinized.

Valerie.ete: From Latin Valeria, feminine form of Valerius.

Veit.ete: From Middle High German Vīt, from Latin Vitus.

Vera.ete: From Russian Ве́ра (Véra) at the end of the 19th century.

Verena.ete: Of obscure origin and meaning; from Verena of Zurzach (near Zurich), a 3rd/4th century saint.

Vincent.ete: Borrowed from French Vincent, from Latin Vincentius.

Volkan.ete: From Turkish Volkan, ultimately from Latin Vulcanus.

Volker.ete: Equivalent to Old High German folc (“people, folk”) (from Proto-West Germanic *folk) + heri (“army”). By surface analysis, Volk + Herr. Cognate to Middle English Fulcher.

Volkert.ete: From Old High German folc + Old High German harti.

Volkhard.ete: From Old High German folc + Old High German harti.

Volkhardt.ete: From Old High German folc + Old High German harti.

Volkhart.ete: From Old High German folc + Old High German harti.

Volkmar.ete: From Old High German *Folkmār, from Proto-West Germanic *Folkmārī, from Proto-Germanic *Fulkamērijaz, equivalent to Old High German folk (“people”) + māri (“famous”).

Volkwin.ete: From Middle High German *Volkewîn, from Old High German *Folkwini, from Proto-West Germanic *Folkawini, equivalent to Old High German folk (“people”) + wini (“friend”).

Waldemar.ete: From an Old High German compound name, from the elements waltan (“rule, govern”) (from Proto-West Germanic *wald) + māri (“famous, great”) (from *mārī). Merged with Scandinavian Valdemar, apparently from the semantically and formally similar Slavic name *Voldiměrъ, which is sometimes considered to also derive from the same pre-Old High German name *waldimӕ̄r-.

Walpurga.ete: Inherited from Old High German Waltburg, from Old High German walt (“rule, authority”) (<< Proto-Germanic *waldaz) + burg (“castle”). The name of the saint is a calque of Old English Wealdburg.

Walter.ete: From Middle High German Walther, from Old High German Waltheri. Cognate with English Walter.
Walter.et: Prénom dont les composés modernes sont walten (« diriger ») et Heer (« armée »).

Waltraud.ete: From the name of a seventh century saint, from Old High German waltan (“rule”) + *þruþi (“strength”).
Waltraud.et: Prénom composé de *waltan et *þruþi dont les équivalents modernes sont walten (« diriger ») et treu (« fidèle »), truth (« vérité »).

Wanja.ete: Borrowed from Russian Ва́ня (Vánja), diminutive of the male name Ива́н (Iván, “John”) and the female name Иванна (Ivanna, “Jane”).

Wendelin.ete: From the name of a sixth century saint, a short form of Germanic compound names beginning with the tribal name Wendel- " a Wend". Compare Dutch Wendelien.

Wenzel.ete: From a diminutive of the name appearing in English as Wenceslaus, from Old Czech Venceslav, from Proto-Slavic *Vęťeslavъ. Doublet of Fatzke.

Werner.ete: Germanic: *waraz (“cautious; heedful; wary; watchful”) + *harjaz (“army; army leader”); roughly equivalent to English Warner.
Werner.et: Du gotique *war(in) (« garde » → voir war en ancien français) et *heri, hari (« armée » → voir herberger en ancien français).

Widukind.ete: Learned borrowing from Old Saxon Widukind.

Wiebke.ete: From a German Low German [Term?] and West Frisian [Term?] diminutive (see -ke) of female given names like Wigburg which begin with Proto-West Germanic *wīg (“battle”). Cognate to Danish Vibeke, Norwegian Vibeke, Swedish Viveca, Viveka.

Wilhardt.ete: From Old High German willo + Old High German harti.

Wilhelm.ete: From Old High German Willahelm from Proto-Germanic *Wiljahelmaz.
Wilhelm.et: Composé de Wille (« volonté ») et de Helm (« heaume », au figuré « protection »).

Wilhelmina.ete: Originating in the 17th century as a feminine form of Wilhelm.

Wilhelmine.et: Dérivé de Wilhelm, avec le suffixe -in.

Willert.ete: A variant of Wilhardt with the h being dropped and the final syllable being weakened. From Old High German willo + Old High German harti.

Witold.ete: Uncertain. From Lithuanian Vytautas or Old High German witu (“wood”) + Old High German waltan.

Wittekind.ete: From Middle High German Witekint, from Old High German *Witukint. Compare Old Saxon Widukind.

Wladimir.ete: From Russian Владимир (Vladimir). Doublet of Waldemar.

Wolf.ete: From Middle High German wolf, from Old High German wolf, from Proto-West Germanic *wulf, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos. Compare Dutch and English wolf, Danish ulv, Gothic 𐍅𐌿𐌻𐍆𐍃 (wulfs).
Wolf.et: Du vieux haut allemand wolf (« loup ») via le moyen haut-allemand wolf ; apparenté à l’anglais wolf, au néerlandais wolf, au suédois ulf, plus loin au vieux slave влькъ → p. ex. le tchèque vlk. De l’indo-européen *wĺ̥kʷos (« loup »), qui donne aussi le latin vulpes, de et lupus → goupil et loup.

Wolfgang.ete: From Middle High German Wolfgang, from Old High German Wolfgang, from wolf (“wolf”) + gang (“path, course”).
Wolfgang.et: Composé de Wolf et de Gang.

Wolfram.ete: From Old High German wolf (“wolf”) + hraban (“raven”).

Wotan.ete: Learned borrowing from Old High German Wodan, from Proto-West Germanic *Wōdan, from Proto-Germanic *Wōdanaz. Cognate with English Woden, Norwegian Nynorsk, Danish, and Swedish Oden, and Icelandic Óðinn. Doublet of Odin.

Xaver.ete: From Spanish Xavier (older spelling of Javier), after 16th-century Catholic saint Francis Xavier.
